entry: Allied offensive of the First World War in northern France, fought from July 1 to November 18, 1916, by the [[British Empire]] and French forces against the [[German Empire]]. More than three million men fought, and more than one million were wounded or killed. The 57,470 British casualties on the first day, including 19,240 killed, were the worst in the history of the British Army. British and French forces penetrated 6.2 miles (10 km) into German-occupied territory but failed to capture Péronne and Bapaume. [[Tank|Tanks]] were used for the first time in September, but proved unreliable.

Ambush of AD 9 in which an alliance of [[Germanic peoples]] annihilated three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus. The alliance was led by [[Arminius]], a Germanic chieftain and officer of Varus's auxiliaries who had received Roman citizenship and military training, and who used that knowledge to anticipate Roman tactics. The battle ended the expansion under [[Augustus]] and dissuaded Rome from conquering Germania. The Rhine became the border of the [[Roman Empire]], and Rome made no major incursion into Germania until [[Marcus Aurelius]] during the Marcomannic Wars.

First major clashes of the [[American Revolutionary War]], fought on April 19, 1775, between British Regulars and Patriot [[Militia|militias]] in Massachusetts. British troops under Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith, sent to seize colonial military supplies at Concord, first fought militia at Lexington, where eight militiamen were killed. Militia fire harassed the British return march to [[Boston]] throughout the day. Casualties totaled 273 for the British and 95 for the colonists. The Continental Congress then formed the Continental Army under [[George Washington]], and militias began the siege of Boston.

Soviet silent epic film of 1925, directed by [[Sergei Eisenstein]], with Grigori Alexandrov as co-director. *Battleship Potemkin* dramatizes the 1905 mutiny aboard the Imperial Russian [[Battleship|battleship]] *Potemkin*, whose crew rebelled against their officers over maggot-infested meat. Commissioned by the Soviet government for the 20th anniversary of the events, it is a prime example of Soviet montage theory. Its "Odessa Steps" sequence, in which [[Cossacks]] fire on a crowd, became widely influential and often recreated, but the massacre it depicts is largely fictional, as no such coordinated slaughter occurred there. The film was banned in several countries, including [[Nazi Germany]] and Britain until 1954. In the 2022 *Sight and Sound* critics' poll it ranked 54th among the greatest films of all time.

Heavily armored warship with a main battery of large-caliber guns, designed as a capital ship. Battleships, among the largest and most formidable warships built from the late 1880s, descended from the sailing [[Ship of the line|ship of the line]] through steam and ironclad designs. Dozens of pre-dreadnoughts were built in the 1890s and early 1900s. In 1906 the British launched the all-big-gun [[Dreadnought]], starting a naval arms race. In the only major fleet engagement of [[World War I]], the [[Battle of Jutland]] in 1916, neither side achieved a decisive result. Interwar treaties, beginning with the Washington Naval Treaty, limited construction. The rise of the [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carrier]] in [[World War II]] relegated battleships to secondary duties, though they fought at the [[Battle of Leyte Gulf]] in 1944. After the war most were placed in reserve, broken up or used as targets. A number of battleships, predominantly American, remain as museum ships.

Mongol ruler and first khan of the [[Golden Horde]] (r. 1227–1255). Batu was a son of [[Jochi]] and, officially, a grandson of [[Genghis Khan]], though Jochi's paternity is highly uncertain. His ulus ruled [[Kievan Rus']], [[Volga Bulgaria]], Cumania and the [[Caucasus]] for around 250 years. In 1235 he was assigned an army of possibly 130,000 for an invasion of Europe, which was in practice commanded by [[Subutai]]. Mongol forces besieged [[Vladimir-Suzdal]] in 1238, taking the city and burning it to the ground, and they annihilated Ryazan after six days of battle. In 1241 Batu's forces crushed Hungarian and Polish armies at Mohi and Legnica. The campaign halted with the death of Ögedei, after which Batu withdrew to secure succession claims. He established his capital at Sarai on the lower Volga.

German art school (1919–1933) that combined crafts and the fine arts. Founded by architect [[Walter Gropius]] in Weimar, it aimed to unify artistic vision with [[Mass production|mass production]] and an emphasis on function. It moved to Dessau in 1925 and to Berlin in 1932, and its leadership closed it in 1933 under Nazi pressure. Its staff included [[Paul Klee]] and [[Wassily Kandinsky]]. The Bauhaus style became one of the most influential currents in modern design and architecture.

Sedimentary rock with a high [[Aluminium|aluminium]] content, and the principal commercial source of aluminium and [[Gallium|gallium]]. It consists mostly of aluminium minerals, including gibbsite (Al(OH)₃) and boehmite (γ-AlO(OH)), mixed with iron oxides and the clay mineral [[Kaolinite]]. Bauxite is reddish-brown, white or tan, with a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Its name derives from its discovery in 1821 by French geologist Pierre Berthier near Les Baux in [[Provence]], southern France. Lateritic bauxite forms through weathering of silicate rocks such as [[Basalt]]. Bauxite is processed by the Bayer process, in which it is heated with [[Sodium hydroxide]] solution to dissolve the aluminium, and the resulting alumina is reduced by [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]]. In 2023, global output reached approximately 390 million metric tons, led by Australia, Guinea and China.

Landlocked state of southeastern [[Germany]], the largest German state by area at 70,550 sq km. Its capital and largest city is [[Munich]], and it has 13.08 million inhabitants. Celtic tribes settled the region in the Iron Age, and it was incorporated into the Roman provinces of Raetia and Noricum in the 1st century AD. The Duchy of Bavaria was created in AD 555. Within the [[Holy Roman Empire]] it gained elector status in 1623 during the [[Thirty Years' War]]. It became the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806 and remained a kingdom within the German Empire until the end of [[World War I]]. The modern state was established in 1945 and became part of [[West Germany]] in 1949. Bavaria is among the wealthiest regions in Germany and Europe, with strengths in manufacturing, engineering and research. Its Catholic heritage shapes its culture, including the [[Oktoberfest]] in Munich.

Recessed coastal body of water that directly connects to an ocean, lake or larger bay. A large bay is usually called a gulf, sea, sound or bight, and a [[Fjord|fjord]] is an elongated bay formed by glacial action. A bay can be the [[Estuary|estuary]] of a river, such as Chesapeake Bay. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea defines a bay as an indentation whose area is at least that of the semicircle drawn across its mouth. Bays form through [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]] and by coastal erosion from rivers and glaciers. The largest bays arose as the supercontinent [[Pangaea]] broke apart, including the [[Bay of Bengal]]. Bays were historically important for fisheries and sea trade, since their sheltered anchorages made them [[Port|ports]].

Northeastern part of the [[Indian Ocean]], between the [[Indian subcontinent]] and the Indochinese peninsula. It covers 2,600,000 sq km (1,000,000 sq mi), making it the world's largest bay. It is bounded by India to the west and northwest, Bangladesh to the north, Myanmar to the northeast, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands of India to the east. Major rivers, including the [[Ganges]], Brahmaputra, Irrawaddy and Godavari, flow into the bay, which receives more than one billion tons of sediment annually. Its coast includes the [[Sundarbans]], the largest mangrove forest in the world. The bay generates about five to six [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]] a year, and its fisheries yield around six million tons of catch annually.

Gulf of the northeast [[Atlantic Ocean]] located south of the Celtic Sea. It lies along the northern coast of Spain and the western coast of France, where it is known as the Gulf of Gascony. Its average depth is 1,744 m (5,722 ft) and its greatest depth 4,735 m (15,535 ft). Parts of the continental shelf extend far into the bay, leaving fairly shallow waters in many areas and rough seas, and heavy storms occur there, especially in winter. The [[Gulf Stream]] enters the bay and keeps temperatures moderate all year. Major cities on its shores include [[Bordeaux]], [[Nantes]], [[Bilbao]] and San Sebastián. In 1592 the Spanish defeated an English fleet during the Battle of the Bay of Biscay.

Failed landing on Cuba's southwestern coast in April 1961, carried out by Cuban exiles and financed directly by the [[United States]]. Brigade 2506, trained by the [[Central Intelligence Agency]] in Guatemala, landed at Playa Girón on April 17. President [[John F. Kennedy]] withheld promised air support, and the invaders were defeated within three days and surrendered on April 20. The failure solidified the position of [[Fidel Castro]] and pushed Cuba toward the [[Soviet Union]], setting the stage for the [[Cuban Missile Crisis]] in 1962.

Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria (r. 1260–1277). Of Turkic Kipchak origin, he was sold into slavery during the Mongol invasions and entered Mamluk service in Egypt. In 1250 he commanded the Muslim forces that captured [[Louis IX of France]] during the Seventh Crusade. He led the vanguard at the Battle of Ain Jalut, the first substantial defeat of the Mongols, and then orchestrated the assassination of Sultan Qutuz to seize the throne. As sultan, he campaigned against the [[Crusader states]], capturing Antioch in 1268, and forged an alliance with the [[Golden Horde]] while engaging the [[Ilkhanate]]. In 1276 he subjugated Makuria in [[Nubia]].

Mathematical rule for inverting conditional probabilities, allowing the probability of a cause to be found from its effect. For example, it gives the probability that a patient has a disease given a positive test, from the probability of a positive test when the disease is present. In symbols, P(A∣B) = P(B∣A)P(A)/P(B). Named after Thomas Bayes, whose essay was published posthumously in 1763, the theorem was developed in the 18th century by Bayes and independently by [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]]. It underlies [[Bayesian inference]], which uses it to update the probability of a hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Harold Jeffreys wrote in 1973 that it "is to the theory of probability what the [[Pythagorean theorem]] is to geometry."

Method of statistical inference that uses [[Bayes' theorem]] to update the probability of a hypothesis as more information becomes available. It combines a prior distribution with the likelihood function of a statistical model for observed data to produce a posterior probability. Bayesian updating is particularly important in the analysis of a sequence of data. The method has been applied in science, engineering, philosophy, [[Medicine|medicine]], sport, [[Psychology|psychology]] and [[Law|law]]. In decision theory it is closely related to subjective probability. Unlike [[Confidence interval|confidence intervals]] in frequentist methods, Bayesian approaches yield credible intervals that express the probability of parameter values.

Theory of statistics based on treating probability as a degree of belief. It codifies prior knowledge as a [[Probability distribution|prior distribution]] and uses [[Bayes' theorem]] to update probabilities after new data are obtained. This contrasts with the frequentist view of probability as the limit of a relative frequency after many trials. Many statisticians viewed Bayesian methods unfavorably for much of the 20th century, but computing advances such as Markov chain Monte Carlo methods gave them prominence in the 21st century.

Embroidered linen cloth nearly 70 metres (230 feet) long, depicting the events leading to the [[Norman Conquest]] of England. Despite its name, it is an embroidery rather than a true [[Tapestry|tapestry]], with images stitched in wool thread on a coarse [[Linen|linen]] ground. Its 58 scenes, with Latin inscriptions, run from 1064 to the [[Battle of Hastings]] in 1066, when [[William the Conqueror|William, Duke of Normandy]] defeated Harold Godwinson. It is generally thought to have been commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux and made in England in the years after the Conquest. Although it presents the Conquest favorably to William, some historians read it as propaganda, and it remains a major source on 11th-century life. It has been inscribed on [[UNESCO]]'s Memory of the World Register since 2007. It is on loan to the [[British Museum]] in London from September 2026, its first time outside France, and is due to return by July 2027.

Burmese king of the [[Toungoo dynasty]] (r. 1550–1581). He assembled the largest empire in Southeast Asian history, encompassing much of present-day [[Myanmar]], the Shan States, [[Lan Xang]], [[Manipur]] and the [[Ayutthaya Kingdom]]. His most enduring legacy was the integration of the Shan States into the Irrawaddy valley administrative system after conquering them between 1557 and 1563. His reforms reduced the power of hereditary Shan rulers, and successive Burmese monarchs followed his model until 1885. The empire was held through personal allegiance to him rather than through institutions, and it collapsed after his death in 1581, when all vassal states had declared independence by 1599. In Thailand he is remembered as "Conqueror of the Ten Directions."

Bladed weapon designed to be mounted on the end of a [[Rifle|rifle]], [[Musket|musket]] or similar long firearm, allowing it to be used as a spear in close combat. From the early 17th to the 20th century it was an [[Infantry|infantry]] melee weapon used in mass charges. The first recorded bayonet appears in the Chinese military treatise *Binglu*, published in 1606. Early plug bayonets fitted directly into the barrel, which made the musket impossible to fire while attached. The later socket bayonet slipped over the muzzle without blocking the bore, allowing soldiers to fire and then charge; French forces adopted it by the 1670s. It proved decisive in conflicts such as the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. Today many armed forces consider bayonets a weapon of last resort, but they are used for parades, crowd control and as utility knives.

American drama television series about lifeguards in Los Angeles County and Hawaii, starring [[David Hasselhoff]]. It was canceled after one season on [[NBC]] but survived in syndication. The show ran as *Baywatch* from 1989 to 1999 and as *Baywatch: Hawaii* from 1999 to 2001. It became the most-watched television series in the world, with more than 1.1 billion weekly viewers, despite consistently negative critical reviews. Its large rotating cast included [[Pamela Anderson]], and its spin-off *Baywatch Nights* aired from 1995 to 1997.

Man-portable, unguided, recoilless antitank rocket launcher widely deployed by the United States Army during [[World War II]]. It fired high-explosive anti-tank (HEAT) shaped-charge warheads against armored vehicles and bunkers at ranges beyond that of a thrown grenade. Germany copied it as the *Panzerschreck*. The M20 Super Bazooka replaced the earlier models during the [[Korean War]]. The nickname came from the M1 variant's vague resemblance to a musical instrument popularized by comedian Bob Burns in the 1930s, and the term now informally denotes any shoulder-fired missile weapon.

Landform of loose particles alongside a body of water. Beach particles are typically rock, such as [[Sand|sand]], gravel, shingle and pebbles, or biological material such as mollusc shells or [[Algae|coralline algae]]. Most beaches are coastal, where wave or current action deposits and reworks [[Sediment|sediment]], though some form on lakes and rivers. Beaches may be backed by coastal [[Dune|dunes]] that offer protection. Many beaches are popular for recreation and [[Tourism|tourism]], and some have lifeguard posts, showers and hospitality venues. Preserved beaches serve as breeding grounds for [[Sea turtle|sea turtles]] and nesting areas for seabirds and penguins. Some estimates describe as much as 50% of the world's sandy beaches disappearing by 2100 because of [[Climate change|climate change]]-driven sea level rise. Human activity, including construction on dunes and [[Water pollution|water pollution]], has also changed beaches.

Team sport, a variant of [[Volleyball|volleyball]] played on [[Sand|sand]] courts divided by a net by two teams of two to six players. Teams may touch the ball up to three times to return it over the net, and the aim is to ground it on the opponent's side. Indoor volleyball was invented in 1895 by William G. Morgan, and the beach game probably originated in 1915 on Waikiki Beach in [[Hawaii]]. The modern two-player game is credited to Paul Johnson of the Santa Monica Athletic Club, who in 1930 played the first recorded doubles game with four players. The sport grew in popularity in the United States during the [[Great Depression]], as it was inexpensive. It has been an Olympic sport since the 1996 Summer Olympics, and the two-player version is the only one contested at an elite level.

British breed of small scent hound, bred for hunting hares and rabbits. Its origin is uncertain, but in the 11th century [[William the Conqueror]] brought the St. Hubert and Talbot hounds to Britain. The modern breed was developed around the 1830s from several breeds, including the Talbot Hound, the North Country Beagle and the Southern Hound. Miniature Beagle-type dogs were kept in the time of [[Edward II]] and [[Elizabeth I]]. Its sense of smell makes it a detection dog for prohibited agricultural imports in quarantine, and it is commonly kept as a companion dog.
